analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited 'soft money' to national party committees, triples individual donor limits, and requires disclosure of issue-advocacy ads.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred national political party committees from soliciting or spending 'soft money' — contributions not subject to federal limits, such as corporate and union money — for federal elections [S2] [S3]. To balance that ban, it would have tripled the individual contribution limit to a federal candidate from $1,000 to $3,000 and indexed it to inflation [S2] [S3]. It also would have required anyone spending more than $10,000 a year on broadcast ads that name a federal candidate shortly before an election to file detailed reports with the Federal Election Commission within 48 hours [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain more visibility into who pays for campaign ads and parties: the bill requires penalty-of-perjury disclosure of contributors behind electioneering communications, including donors of $3,000 or more to issue-advocacy groups [S3]. Banning soft money would close the channel through which corporations, unions, and wealthy donors could give unlimited, largely unregulated money to national party committees for federal elections [S2] [S3]. The higher individual limits, combined with inflation indexing, modestly benefit candidates who can raise money from a broad base of donors and free candidates from relying on party soft-money operations [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates relying on disclosed funds

how_it_helps.text: Bans national party committees and their agents from soliciting, receiving, or spending money not subject to federal contribution limits and reporting rules, closing the unlimited 'soft money' channel for federal elections.

Requires state and local party committees to pay for federal election activity — including voter registration drives, get-out-the-vote efforts, and ads mentioning federal candidates — only with federally limited, reported funds.

Requires anyone spending over $10,000 a year on 'electioneering communications' — TV or radio ads naming a federal candidate within 60 days of a general election or 30 days of a primary — to file a 48-hour report under penalty of perjury identifying the spender and its $3,000-plus donors, and disclosing coordination with candidates or parties.
Bars party committees from soliciting funds for or directing donations to tax-exempt 501(c) organizations, a common way to route money around campaign rules.

analysis.who_pays: National party committees lose their largest fundraising tool, since soft money — including corporate and union contributions not subject to federal limits — is banned for federal election activity [S2] [S3]. Wealthy individuals and organized interests lose the ability to influence federal elections through unlimited party contributions and unreported issue ads, though wealthy individuals gain in one respect: they can legally give three times as much directly to candidates, with automatic increases for inflation [S3]. Broadcast advertisers and issue-advocacy groups face new reporting burdens on pre-election ads [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill triples the individual contribution limit from $1,000 to $3,000 and indexes it to inflation, so the wealthiest donors can legally give a candidate three times as much — a direct benefit to people of means and to candidates with access to them.

The bill addresses issue-advocacy ads with disclosure only, not limits: unlimited spending on pre-election ads naming federal candidates remains legal as long as it is reported, leaving the money in politics rather than removing it.

Higher individual limits can advantage candidates with strong networks of wealthy donors, and can be argued to help incumbents and well-funded challengers alike, while candidates who rely on small donors gain little from a $3,000 ceiling they could not approach anyway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core — banning soft money and requiring public disclosure of pre-election issue ads — addresses real loopholes that let unlimited, lightly reported money flow into federal elections. But the bill's design is a genuine trade: it buys off the loss of soft money by letting wealthy individuals triple their direct contributions and locking in automatic increases. Critics could fairly say it shifts influence from parties to the same large donors, rather than reducing the role of big money overall.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, vote, or floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill for herself and Senator Robert Torricelli on March 22, 2000.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration.
No further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — appears in the record for the remainder of the 106th Congress, which ended January 3, 2001.

The referral placed the bill in the committee chaired by Senator Mitch McConnell, the Senate's most prominent opponent of campaign-finance limits; under his chairmanship the committee never acted on it.

This was part of a broader pattern: comprehensive campaign-finance legislation in that era, including the parallel McCain-Feingold effort, repeatedly stalled in the Senate before finally passing as the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees, big individual donors, and the corporations, unions, and interest groups that funded parties and issue ads through unlimited soft money are better off, because no restrictions took effect and unlimited soft money continued to flow through the 2000 elections. Voters gained nothing: no ban, no expanded disclosure, and limits stayed at $1,000.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: National parties, large donors, and issue advertisers

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban soft money, raise individual contribution limits, and require disclosure of issue-advocacy ads, then saw it referred to committee with no further action.

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor; the bill was introduced on his behalf alongside Feinstein's.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it out, held no vote, and allowed it to die at the end of the 106th Congress.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled action on the bill; he was the Senate's best-known opponent of campaign-finance limits and led the fights against McCain-Feingold in the same period.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought campaign-finance legislation, including this bill, to the Senate floor; the majority leader controlled which bills reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic sponsors and was sent to a committee chaired by Senator Mitch McConnell, the Republican leading opposition to campaign-finance limits, and the Republican-led Senate never acted on it; no roll-call votes were ever taken.

industries.note: The bill bans their unlimited soft-money fundraising for federal elections but compensates by tripling the hard-money limit donors can give through them and to candidates. Parties profited by channeling unlimited corporate and union money into federal campaigns, which the public could not see or limit.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and wealthy households
industries.note: Their direct giving ceiling rises from $1,000 to $3,000 per candidate with automatic inflation increases. Their interest in greater giving power runs against the public's interest in limiting the influence of big money.

industries.industry: Corporations and unions using soft money
industries.note: Soft money let them pour unlimited funds into national party committees for federal election activity despite bans on their direct contributions. The bill shuts that channel for parties, though not for their own independent issue-advocacy ads.
Party committees could no longer solicit funds for or direct donations to 501(c) groups, cutting off a route for moving party-linked money outside federal limits and disclosure.

They gain no spending rights they lacked but face rapid, detailed reporting — under penalty of perjury — of pre-election TV and radio ads naming federal candidates, including their major donors. Unlimited spending stays legal; only secrecy ends.

Higher, inflation-indexed individual limits favor candidates with access to donor networks, which incumbents typically have. Officeholders deciding their own campaign-finance rules stand to benefit from the provision they control.
